strengths: Comprehensive and systematic expressivity theory for weight-space networks filling an important theoretical gap
Novel architectural equivalence results (Theorem 5.2) showing diverse weight-space networks are equally expressive
Sophisticated technical contributions including canonization maps, neuron identification, and careful treatment of weight vs. function-space expressivity
Well-motivated four-fold classification of approximation settings with real-world examples
Important negative results (Propositions 7.1, 6.2) revealing expressivity limitations and guiding future architecture design
Natural general-position assumption (distinct layer biases) proven to hold almost surely for random initialization
Technically sound proofs with no apparent errors; careful handling of subtle issues like finite-precision regimes
weaknesses: Entirely theoretical work lacking any empirical validation of core predictions (e.g., scaling behavior in Theorem 7.2, general position in practice)
Limited practical guidance—results characterize approximation capability but offer little actionable direction for practitioners or architects
Significant gap between theory (continuous weights, compact domains, asymptotic analysis) and practice (finite precision, unbounded spaces, finite samples)
Theorem 7.2 requires 'sufficiently large' architecture but provides no quantitative bounds or sample complexity analysis
No analysis of optimization or learning dynamics; expressivity alone does not characterize practical learnability
Dense 62-page presentation with rushed main text; key intuitions (especially regarding general position necessity) deserve clearer exposition
General position assumption, while natural, excludes quantized/binary networks—brief mention but insufficient treatment
Limited scope: excludes scale-equivariant networks by design and doesn't address extensions to modern architectures (Transformers, CNNs)

strengths: Comprehensive theoretical framework filling a genuine gap in weight-space network expressivity analysis
Four well-motivated approximation settings with practical applications (Figure 2) and clear examples
Technically rigorous results: architectural equivalence (Thm 5.2), universality under natural assumptions (Thms 6.1, 6.3, 7.4), and characterization of limitation regimes (Props 6.2, 7.3)
Natural general-position assumption that is measure-theoretic and practically reasonable, with honest treatment of edge cases
Elegant mathematical techniques: realization map continuity, Weisfeiler-Leman analysis for negative results, canonization maps for symmetry handling
Well-organized presentation with clear contribution landscape (Figure 1) and extensive verified proofs (60+ page appendix)
Results unify disparate prior work and provide principled foundation for future research in weight-space learning
weaknesses: No empirical validation of core claims; universality results lack concrete convergence rates or approximation bounds needed for practice
Incomplete characterization of function-space operators: Theorem 7.2 requires 'sufficiently large architecture' without explicit size bounds as function of operator complexity
Limited practical guidance: results don't translate to actionable recommendations for practitioners choosing between architectures or methods
General position assumption, while natural, may fail for low-precision networks and quantized models—brief treatment of these practical edge cases
Scope restricted to MLPs; unclear how techniques extend to CNNs, Transformers, or other symmetry structures beyond permutations
Critical proofs in appendix (>60 pages) reduces verifiability of main paper; general position definition appears late
Artificial counterexamples (Props 6.2, 7.3) for non-universal cases leave gap between impossibility on full space and possibility on general-position subset
